title: 2 · Strings, Scanner & Conditionals (Deep Dive)
learn:
Strings: a necklace of characters

A String is an object holding a sequence of characters, indexed from 0. It is immutable: methods never change the original, they return a new String. Common methods: length(), charAt(i), indexOf(c), substring(b, e) (includes b, stops before e), toUpperCase(), trim(), equalsIgnoreCase(x). Joining uses +.

The great trap: == vs equals

== compares addresses (is it the very same object?). .equals() compares the text. Two Strings built with new can hold identical text yet be different objects, so == gives false. Rule: always use .equals() to compare Strings.

Scanner: listening to the keyboard

Three steps: import java.util.Scanner, create new Scanner(System.in), call a method: next() (one word), nextInt(), nextDouble(), nextLine() (whole line). The notorious bug: after nextInt() the Enter key is still waiting in the input, so the next nextLine() grabs that empty leftover. Fix: call nextLine() once to throw it away. Close with sc.close().

if / else if / else

Java checks top to bottom and runs only the first true branch. Combine tests with && (and), || (or), ! (not). Comparison operators: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=. A single = assigns, a classic slip. Order matters: test the highest range first (score >= 75 before score >= 50) or every high score lands in the wrong branch.

switch: a menu for exact values

switch compares one value against case labels. break stops execution; without it Java falls through into the next case, which you can use deliberately to share one action between labels (Monday and Tuesday both print “unwind”). default catches everything else. Use if/else for ranges, switch for fixed values.

The ternary shortcut

String r = (score >= 50) ? "Pass" : "Fail"; means: if true take the first value, else the second.
